source.title_on_document: The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking

supplement.where: 'The full study protocol can be found in supplementary material' (p. 4, Section 3.1). No URL given. Appendix A (NASA-TLX means and standard errors, Table A.1) is printed in this PDF (p. 18).
supplement.holds: The full study protocol. All model estimates for the four outcomes (Tables 1-4, pp. 8-10) and Figures 6-9 are in this PDF. The paper does not say that any statistic sits only in the supplement.

paper_design_summary: Sixty participants with visual design experience, recruited through university student channels, were randomly assigned in individual lab sessions to sketch chatbot-avatar ideas on paper for 20 minutes with no inspiration support, with Google Image Search, or with Midjourney V4 (20 per condition), after seeing an example robot avatar meant to induce fixation. Two raters counted the example's features in each of the 277 sketches (design fixation) and grouped the sketches into 83 clusters, which give each participant's variety and each sketch's originality; fluency is the number of sketches. Bayesian models compare each support condition with the no-support baseline.

studies.label: Lab experiment: chatbot-avatar sketching with no support, Google Image Search, or Midjourney V4

assignment.what_was_assigned: Inspiration Stimulus available during the 20-minute sketching task: none (Baseline), Google Image Search (Image Search), or Midjourney V4 (GenAI)
assignment.quote: After completing the questionnaire, the participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions and were assigned a unique ID generated by the computer (3 random digits) (Figure 3-3).
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3.3 Procedure; between-participants design stated on p. 3, Section 3, and p. 4, Section 3.1

arms.name: GenAI
arms.description: Access during the task to the paid version of Midjourney V4 through a private Discord server running the Midjourney bot; each text prompt returned a set of four images; video tutorial on the tool beforehand (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Section 3.3).

arms.name: Image Search
arms.description: Access during the task to Google Images in a browser in incognito mode; video tutorial on the tool beforehand (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Section 3.3).

arms.name: Baseline (No support)
arms.description: No inspiration support; the same written brief, example avatar, drawing materials, and 20-minute limit as the other arms (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Section 3.3).

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper gives 60 participants, randomly assigned to three conditions, with an equal number per condition (10 women and 10 men each, so 20 per arm). It reports no exclusion or dropout. The outcome models (Tables 1-4) do not print their N. The NASA-TLX ANOVA reports F(2, 57) (p. 6), consistent with 60 people. The paper does not say how the exact 10/10 gender balance per condition was reached.
participants.who: Adults (18 or older) with self-described visual design experience, recruited through digital student notice boards, mailing lists of university student clubs, and word of mouth. They included undergraduate, master's, and PhD students from arts, business, computer science and IT, design, engineering, and science; mean age 25.8 (range 18-49, SD 5.4). Few had professional industry experience, and the authors call them novice designers (p. 16).
participants.country: not_stated. The paper says only that the study ran in 'a quiet research laboratory' (p. 6) with 'ethics approval from our university' (p. 3). Four authors are at The University of Melbourne and one at RMIT University, both in Melbourne, Australia (p. 1).
participants.quote: We recruited 60 participants through digital student notice boards, mailing lists of university student clubs, and word of mouth.

ai_tool.name_model: Midjourney V4 (paid version; the default model in May 2023), accessed through the Midjourney bot on a private Discord server
ai_tool.how_used: During the 20-minute task, participants could enter text prompts and view the four images returned per prompt as inspiration while they sketched by hand on paper. GenAI participants wrote 117 prompts in total (mean 5.85 per participant, median 5.5, range 2-15), and the paper inspects the 468 images Midjourney returned (p. 11, Section 4.6.1; p. 12, Section 4.6.2).

task.description: Sketch on paper as many ideas as possible for an avatar for a chatbot described as 'kind, loving, caring, and intelligent'. The written brief included an example robot avatar with 14 salient features, shown to induce design fixation (p. 4, Section 3.1, Figure 1).
task.duration: 20 minutes of sketching; sessions lasted 45-60 minutes in total (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Section 3.3)

outcomes.name: Design fixation score (DFS): share of the example avatar's 14 salient features repeated in each sketch
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters blind to the experiment's aims counted which of the 14 salient features of the example avatar appear in each sketch. DFS = features repeated from the example / fixating features in the example (Eq. 1, p. 5). The raters were HCI researchers with experience teaching and evaluating design (p. 7, Section 3.4). The paper says it computed inter-rater reliability but prints no value. Higher DFS means more copying of the example, so the sign runs against creativity. Bayesian binomial model with 14 trials, a probit link, and random effects for participant and image (p. 8, Section 4.2, Table 1). The paper does not say whether the two raters' counts were combined before modeling. n_units 277 is the total sketch count (p. 5). Of these, 92 come from the GenAI arm (p. 12, Section 4.6.2), and the paper prints no sketch count for the other two arms. The model's N is not printed.

contrasts.reported: Table 1 (probit scale; posterior mean (posterior SD), 89% compatibility interval): GenAI .32 (0.13) [.11, .54]; Intercept -.71 (.10) [-.86, .56] as printed. Text: 'mean = .32, 89% CI [.11, .55]', '100% probability of leading to higher Design Fixation', 'Bayes Factor of 124'. Higher DFS means more copying of the example (less creative). Figure 6 plots arm-level posterior predictions (median ± S.E.) with no printed values.

No GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate or interval is printed. The direction follows the two coefficients against the shared baseline and the text. Table 1: GenAI .32 (0.13) [.11, .54]; Image Search .27 (0.14) [.05, .48] (text: 'mean = .27, 89% CI [.05, .49]', '98% probability', 'Bayes Factor of 42.48'). Text: 'GenAI led to even more design fixation than Image Search'. Figure 6 plots both arms with no printed values.

outcomes.name: Fluency: number of sketches per participant
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of sketches each participant produced in the 20 minutes (Eq. 2, p. 5). Bayesian negative binomial model with a log link; the shape parameter also depends on the stimulus (shape rows of Table 2). Total-effects model: Fluency ~ Stimulus. The direct-effects model adds offset(log(Time on Task)), a post-assignment variable, as a mediation variant (p. 8, Section 4.3). One row per participant; the model's N is not printed. The paper does not say whether the model counts all sketches or sketches minus one, as the variety model does. Table 2's total effects imply about one sketch per participant fewer than the printed totals (92 GenAI sketches, p. 12; 277 in all, p. 5; see notes and open questions).

contrasts.reported: Table 2 total effects (log scale; posterior mean (SD), 89% CI): GenAI -.21 (.30) [-.66, .26]; Intercept 1.50 (.19) [1.20, 1.80]. Text: '89% CI [-.7, .28]', 'Bayes factor of 3.20', '76% posterior probability of a negative effect'. Direct effects (offset for time on task): GenAI .10 (.31) [-.39, .58]; text '89% CI [-.41, .60]', 'Bayes factor of .61', '38% posterior probability of a negative effect'. Both 89% intervals include zero. The paper reads the total effect as negative. Figure 7 plots arm-level posterior predictions (median ± S.E.) with no printed values. Printed arm total: 'the total set of sketches produced by participants in the AI condition (92 in total)' (p. 12, Section 4.6.2), a mean of 4.6 per GenAI participant at 20 per arm (derived, not printed). No Baseline total is printed. Table 2's total effects imply exp(1.50 - .21) = 3.63 sketches per GenAI participant (derived), and Figure 7 plots GenAI at about 3.6, so the printed total and the model differ by about one sketch per participant (see notes).
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Section 4.3, Table 2, Figure 7; p. 12, Section 4.6.2 (92 GenAI sketches)

contrasts.reported: No GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate or interval is printed. The direction follows the two coefficients against the shared baseline. Table 2 total effects: GenAI -.21 (.30) [-.66, .26]; Image Search -.49 (.25) [-.88, -.10] (text: 'mean = -.49, 89% CI [-.9, -.10]', 'Bayes factor of 46.62', '98% posterior probability of a negative effect'). Direct effects: GenAI .10 (.31) [-.39, .58]; Image Search -.22 (.25) [-.63, .17] (text: 'mean = -0.22, 89% CI [-0.64, 0.19]', 'Bayes factor of 4.20'). Text: 'The effect of Image Search is more pronounced'. The conclusion (p. 16) says GenAI gave lower fluency than image search, which conflicts with Table 2. Figure 7 plots both arms with no printed values. The GenAI arm's sketch total is printed (92, p. 12, Section 4.6.2), but no Image Search total is printed. GenAI stays above Image Search whether the model counts all sketches or sketches minus one.
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Section 4.3, Table 2, Figure 7; p. 12, Section 4.6.2; p. 16, Section 6

outcomes.name: Variety: number of idea clusters a participant's sketches fall into
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters blind to the conditions grouped all 277 sketches, shown in random order on a Miro board, into 83 mutually exclusive clusters by appearance, embodiment, appendages, shape, and accessories. Variety = (clusters a participant's sketches belong to - 1) / (number of clusters - 1) (Eq. 3, p. 5); the model uses the count of clusters minus one. Bayesian negative binomial model with a log link. Total-effects model: Variety ~ Stimulus. The direct-effects model adds Fluency as a covariate, a mediation variant (p. 9, Section 4.4). This is variety within one person's sketches, not across people. One row per participant; the model's N is not printed.

contrasts.reported: Table 3 total effects (log scale; posterior mean (SD), 89% CI): GenAI -.29 (-.28) [-.74, .17] (SD printed with a minus sign); Intercept 1.01 (.19) [.71, 1.30]. Text: 'mean = -.29, 89% CI [-.75, .16]', '86% probability of being negative', 'Bayes Factor of 5.93'. Direct effects (Fluency as covariate): GenAI -.15 (0.24) [-.53, .23]; text 'mean = -.15 [-55, .24]' as printed, 'Bayes Factor of 2.64'. Both 89% intervals include zero. The paper reads both effects as negative. Figure 8 plots arm-level posterior predictions (median ± S.E.) with no printed values.

No GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate or interval is printed. The direction follows the two total-effect coefficients against the shared baseline. Table 3 total effects: GenAI -.29 (-.28) [-.74, .17]; Image Search -.39 (.28) [-.84, -.06] (text: 'mean = -.40, [-.87, -.07]', 'Bayes Factor of 11.38'). Text: 'The effect of Image Search was even more negative'. The direct effects run the other way: GenAI -.15 (0.24) [-.53, .23]; Image Search .02 (0.25) [-.38, .42] (text: 'mean = .02 [-.39, .43]'). The conclusion (p. 16) says GenAI gave lower variety than image search, which conflicts with the total effects. Figure 8 plots both arms with no printed values.
contrasts.locator: pp. 9-10, Section 4.4, Table 3, Figure 8; p. 16, Section 6

outcomes.name: Originality: share of other participants without an idea in the same cluster, per sketch
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For each sketch, Originality = 1 - (number of other participants with ideas in the cluster / number of other participants) (Eq. 4, p. 5), using the 83 rater-built clusters over all 277 sketches. The paper defines it against 'the total pool of sketches made by participants' and does not say explicitly whether 'other participants' spans all three conditions. Bayesian linear regression with a participant random effect. Total-effects model: Originality ~ Stimulus + (1|Participant ID). The direct-effects model adds Variety (p. 10, Section 4.5, Table 4). Figure 9 plots values averaged per participant. The score is the rarity of one sketch in the pooled sample, not a within-arm similarity across people, so it is coded novelty. n_units 277 is the total sketch count (p. 5). Of these, 92 come from the GenAI arm (p. 12, Section 4.6.2), and the paper prints no sketch count for the other two arms. The model's N is not printed.

contrasts.reported: Table 4 total effects (posterior mean (SD), 89% CI): GenAI -.03 (.02) [-.06, -.01]; Intercept .86 (.01) [.84, .88]. Text: 'mean = -.03, 89% CI [-.06, .00]', '97% probability of being negative', 'Bayes Factor of 35.' Direct effects (Variety as covariate): GenAI -.03 (0.02) [-.05, -.01]. The authors call the effects of both stimuli 'negligible'. Figure 9 plots arm-level posterior predictions (median ± S.E., averaged per participant) with no printed values.

No GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate or interval is printed. The direction follows the two coefficients against the shared baseline and the text. Table 4 total effects: GenAI -.03 (.02) [-.06, -.01]; Image Search -.01 (.02) [-.04, .01] (text: 'mean = -0.01, [-.04, .01]', 'a Bayes Factor of 3.9 provides only anecdotal evidence against the hypothesis that it has a positive effect'). Direct effects: GenAI -.03 (0.02) [-.05, -.01]; Image Search -.01 (0.02) [-.03, .02]. Text: 'The effect of Image Search was slightly less negative'. The authors call both effects negligible. Figure 9 plots both arms with no printed values.

company_involvement.description: Funded by the Rowden White Scholarship and the Melbourne Research Scholarship (University of Melbourne). Midjourney (paid version) and Google Images were used as tools. No company role is stated.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to Midjourney V4, Google Image Search, or no support (p. 6, Section 3.3). Sixty people were randomized, 20 per arm (p. 5, Section 3.2; p. 6, Section 3.3). The paper reports no exclusion or dropout, so 60 were analyzed. The NASA-TLX ANOVA's F(2, 57) fits 60 people (p. 6), but no outcome model prints its N. That is above the 50 threshold but close to it, and the GenAI vs no-support contrast alone has 40 people. Design fixation, fluency, variety, and originality are scored on the sketches, by raters or from rater-built clusters (p. 5, Section 3.1), and Midjourney was available while participants sketched (p. 4, Section 3.1). The one-sketch gap between the fluency estimates and the printed sketch totals, and the scale of Figure 8, bear on extraction, not on eligibility.

one_line_finding: Compared with no support, Midjourney access raised the design fixation score (probit posterior mean .32, SD 0.13, 89% CI [.11, .54]; Table 1, p. 8) and lowered originality by an amount the authors call negligible (-.03, SD .02, 89% CI [-.06, -.01]; Table 4, p. 10), while the fluency (-.21, [-.66, .26]) and variety (-.29, [-.74, .17]) estimates have 89% intervals that include zero (Tables 2-3, p. 9).
open_questions: Originality is the rarity of a sketch's cluster among other participants in the pooled sample (p. 5). The codebook puts rarity of a single output under novelty, so no across_people outcome is coded. The candidate record says de Rooij and Biskjaer (2026) entered this paper as a group-level homogenization effect digitized from graphs. Review should decide whether originality, or another cluster-based measure, also answers across_people.
Design fixation (copying of the example's 14 features; higher is worse) is coded construct 'other'. Review should decide whether it enters as a reverse-signed novelty measure or stays apart.

All estimates are Bayesian posterior means with posterior SDs and 89% compatibility intervals on probit, log, and linear scales. These intervals are narrower than the 95% intervals in most other papers. The only printed arm-level value for any outcome is the GenAI sketch total (92 sketches, p. 12). Other arm levels appear only as plotted posterior predictions in Figures 6-9. No participant-level SD is printed for any outcome, and no GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate is printed. Figures 6, 7, and 9 match their tables, but Figure 8 is not on the Eq. 3 scale (last open question). Extraction would need to digitize Figures 6, 7, and 9 or ask the authors for arm means and SDs.
The paper describes random assignment in one sentence (p. 6) and does not say how exactly 10 women and 10 men reached each condition (p. 5). The balance suggests assignment stratified by gender.
No outcome model prints its N. n_units 277 is the total sketch count (p. 5), and the paper does not say whether the design fixation model has one row per sketch or one per rater.

The fluency estimates and the printed sketch totals differ by about one sketch per participant. Table 2's total effects imply exp(1.50) = 4.48, exp(1.50 - .49) = 2.75, and exp(1.50 - .21) = 3.63 sketches per participant in the Baseline, Image Search, and GenAI arms, and Figure 7 plots 4.47, 2.75, and 3.62 (read from the PDF's vector paths). At 20 per arm that is about 217 sketches, but p. 5 counts 277, and p. 12 counts 92 GenAI sketches (4.6 per participant). A fluency model of sketches minus one, as the variety model is (p. 9), would fit all three printed totals (20 x (5.48 + 3.75 + 4.63) = 277.2, against 277 printed), but Eq. 2 says 'Number of sketches produced by the participant'. Until the authors clarify, Table 2's coefficients should not be read as log ratios of sketch counts. The coded directions do not change: the GenAI vs Baseline interval includes zero on either reading, and GenAI stays above Image Search.

Figure 8 plots variety at 0.080 (Baseline), 0.054 (Image Search), and 0.060 (GenAI), read from the PDF's vector paths, on an axis labeled 'Percentage of clusters'. Table 3's total effects put these arms at exp(1.01)/82 = 0.034, exp(.62)/82 = 0.023, and exp(.72)/82 = 0.025 on the Eq. 3 scale. Each plotted level is about 2.4 times the Eq. 3 value, while the ratios between arms agree with Table 3 (0.676 vs exp(-.39) = 0.677; 0.751 vs exp(-.29) = 0.748). Each sketch belongs to exactly one cluster, and GenAI participants averaged 4.6 sketches (p. 12), so the GenAI arm cannot average above (4.6 - 1)/82 = 0.044 on Eq. 3, or above 4.6/83 = 0.055 on the caption's 'percentage of clusters in which the participant has sketches'. The paper does not say what Figure 8 divides by, so digitized Figure 8 levels are not Eq. 3 variety.
notes: Single study with three arms sharing one baseline. No outcome is measured after AI was removed. The outcome order follows the paper (design fixation, fluency, variety, originality), as in form B; form A listed the same four outcomes in reverse order. Printed inconsistencies are recorded as printed. Table 1 gives the intercept interval as [-.86, .56], and the upper bound's sign looks like a typo. Design fixation: GenAI [.11, .54] in Table 1 vs [.11, .55] in the text, Image Search [.05, .48] vs [.05, .49]. Fluency: GenAI total [-.66, .26] in Table 2 vs [-.7, .28] in the text, GenAI direct [-.39, .58] vs [-.41, .60], Image Search total [-.88, -.10] vs [-.9, -.10], Image Search direct [-.63, .17] vs [-0.64, 0.19]. Fluency levels: p. 12 prints 92 sketches for the GenAI arm (4.6 per participant at 20 per arm), but Table 2's total effects imply 3.63 per GenAI participant, and Figure 7 plots 3.62. Across arms, Table 2 implies about 217 sketches at 20 per arm, against the 277 on p. 5. Both gaps equal about one sketch per participant (open questions). Variety: Table 3 prints the GenAI total SD as (-.28); GenAI total [-.74, .17] vs [-.75, .16] in the text, GenAI direct [-.53, .23] vs '[-55, .24]', Image Search total -.39 [-.84, -.06] vs -.40 [-.87, -.07], Image Search direct [-.38, .42] vs [-.39, .43]. Originality: GenAI total [-.06, -.01] in Table 4 vs [-.06, .00] in the text. The originality paragraph says 'a negative effect on the variety of output', calls a Bayes Factor of 35 'extreme evidence', and calls 3.9 'only anecdotal'. The paper's own scale (p. 8) puts values under 100 at 'very strong' and values under 10 at 'substantial'. The abstract and conclusion describe fewer ideas and less variety with AI, but the 89% intervals of those total effects include zero, so their directions are coded no_clear_difference. The conclusion (p. 16) also says GenAI gave lower fluency and variety than image search, which conflicts with the total-effect point estimates in Tables 2-3. Not listed as outcomes: the within-GenAI Spearman correlation (rho = 0.56) between each sketch's DFS and the DFS of the AI images seen just before it (82 of 92 GenAI sketches; 10 were drawn before any prompt; p. 12, Figure 10), which is not an arm contrast; the share of AI images resembling the example (44 percent, 206/468, p. 12) and the prompt word counts (Table 5, p. 11), which describe AI inputs and outputs; NASA-TLX workload, self-reported, with no difference by condition (F(2, 57) = 1, p = 0.37; p. 6; Table A.1, p. 18); and the qualitative interview analysis. Standard-error basis: the design fixation and originality models have one row per sketch with participant random effects (design fixation also has an image random effect); the fluency and variety models have one row per participant. The paper says Figures 6-9 plot posterior predictions on the normalized scales of Section 3.1, while the models use the original counts (p. 8). Read from the PDF's vector paths, Figures 6, 7, and 9 match their tables: Figure 6 plots .240, .329, and .350 against Phi(-.71) = .239, Phi(-.44) = .330, and Phi(-.39) = .348; Figure 7 plots 4.47, 2.75, and 3.62 sketches against 4.48, 2.75, and 3.63; Figure 9 plots .860, .853, and .830 against .86, .85, and .83. Figure 8 does not: its levels are about 2.4 times the Eq. 3 values that Table 3 implies (open questions). The markdown tables match the PDF; the markdown omits the figures and places references 64-73 after the appendix. Every number here was checked against the PDF pages. The final review added the GenAI sketch total (p. 12) and the figure readings, which come from the PDF's vector paths, not from printed values.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O2 fluency and open_questions[2]: the form said arm-level values appear only as plotted predictions in Figures 6-9, but p. 12 prints the GenAI arm's sketch total (92, so 4.6 per participant at 20 per arm). This conflicts with Table 2's total-effects level, exp(1.50 - .21) = 3.63, and with Figure 7 (about 3.6). Across arms, Table 2 implies about 217 sketches against the 277 on p. 5. The conflict was missing from 'reported' and from the notes.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Confirmed on PDF pp. 5, 9, and 12. Figure 7, read from the PDF's vector paths, plots 4.47, 2.75, and 3.62 sketches, which match Table 2, while 92/20 = 4.6. Recorded the printed total in 'reported' for both S1-O2 contrasts and in the measure_detail of S1-O1, S1-O2, and S1-O4 (92 of the 277 sketches are from the GenAI arm). Added the conflict to the notes and as a new open question, which says that a model of sketches minus one would fit all printed totals (277.2 vs 277) but the paper does not say so. Rewrote open_questions[2]: the GenAI sketch total is the only printed arm-level value. No code changed. The GenAI vs Baseline direction rests on the Table 2 interval, and GenAI stays above Image Search on either reading.
challenge_resolution.quote: For this analysis, we begin with the total set of sketches produced by participants in the AI condition (92 in total).
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 12, Section 4.6.2; p. 9, Table 2 (Total Effects) and Figure 7; p. 5, Section 3.1 (N=277, Eq. 2)

challenge_resolution.problem: Figure 8 and open_questions[2]: Figure 8 plots variety at about 0.080, 0.054, and 0.060 (Baseline, Image Search, GenAI) on an axis labeled 'Percentage of clusters', about 2.4 times the Eq. 3 values that Table 3's total effects imply (0.034, 0.023, 0.025). The notes repeated the paper's claim that the plots use the Section 3.1 scales, and open_questions[2] proposed digitizing Figures 6-9 with no warning about Figure 8.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Confirmed from the PDF's vector paths: Figure 8 plots 0.0802, 0.0542, and 0.0602, which are 2.39 to 2.40 times exp(1.01)/82 = 0.0335, exp(.62)/82 = 0.0227, and exp(.72)/82 = 0.0251. The ratios between arms match Table 3, and Figures 6, 7, and 9 match their tables. Added the warning to the notes and to open_questions[2], and added a new open question on what Figure 8 divides by. One adjustment to the checker's argument: (277/60 - 1)/82 = 0.044 bounds the pooled mean, not each arm. The form uses the GenAI-arm ceiling from the printed 92 sketches, (4.6 - 1)/82 = 0.044, which the plotted 0.060 exceeds. No recorded estimate or code changed.
challenge_resolution.quote: We built our models based on the original count data in the direct measurements but report normalised values as described in Section 3.1 in our plots for easier comparisons with future work.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 8 and Table 3 (Total Effects); p. 5, Section 3.1 (Eq. 3, 83 clusters)

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: whether originality (the rarity of a sketch's cluster among other participants, p. 5), or another cluster-based measure, also answers across_people. This is a codebook call for Review 1 on a measure the paper defines. The paper also does not say whether 'other participants' spans all three arms. Only the authors could say, and the coding needs it only if Review wants a within-arm measure.

open_questions[1]: whether design fixation (copying of the example's 14 features, higher is worse) enters as a reverse-signed novelty measure or stays apart as 'other'. This is a codebook call for Review 1.

open_questions[2]: the paper prints no participant-level SD, no arm mean except the GenAI sketch total (92), and no GenAI-minus-Image-Search estimate. Standardized effects need digitized Figures 6, 7, and 9 or the authors' numbers. The paper links no data or code.

open_questions[3]: how exactly 10 women and 10 men reached each arm (about a 5 percent chance under complete randomization), which points to randomization within gender. Criterion 1 stays met: the paper states random assignment (p. 6), and randomization within strata still qualifies. The full study protocol in the supplementary material (p. 4) may describe the allocation.

open_questions[4]: no outcome model prints its N, and the paper does not say whether the design fixation model has one row per sketch or one per rater. Criterion 2 rests on 60 people with no reported loss (per-participant scoring, F(2, 57), 117 prompts at 5.85 per GenAI participant), so this bears on standard errors, not on eligibility.

open_questions[5]: Table 2's fluency levels sit about one sketch per participant below the printed totals (3.63 vs 4.6 per GenAI participant; about 217 vs 277 sketches in all). A model of sketches minus one would fit, but the paper does not say so. The coded directions hold on either reading.

open_questions[6]: what Figure 8 divides by. Its variety levels are about 2.4 times the Eq. 3 values that Table 3 implies, so Figure 8 should not be digitized for arm levels until the authors explain it.
